newsitem.title: USA: Whitman to spin off Midas, Hussmann.
newsitem.headline: Whitman to spin off Midas, Hussmann.

text.p: Whitman Corp. said Monday it plans to spin off its Midas International unit, the world's largest automotive service franchise, enabling it to focus on its giant Pepsi-Cola bottling business.
Whitman also set plans to spin off Hussman Corp., the largest supplier of refrigeration systems for the food industry, with annual sales of about $1 billion.

"We've been considering an action like this for a fair bit of time," said Charles Connolly, vice president of corporate affairs and investor relations. "That has led us to believe this is a good time to get on with it."

After the planned spin-offs, Whitman will concentrate on Pepsi-Cola General, the world's largest independent Pepsi-Cola franchisee, which accounts for half of Whitman's sales and more than half of its operating income.
"The era of the conglomerate is apparently on its way out," Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette analyst Skip Carpenter said of the planned spin-offs.
"I think it's the right move at the right time," said Salomon Bros. analyst Jennifer Solomon.
Whitman stock jumped $2.25 to $25.625 on the New York Stock Exchange in afternoon trading.
"We believe that as independent publicly traded companies, our businesses will realise a number of benefits," Whitman Chairman Bruce Chelberg said in a statement.
Going forward, Pepsi-Cola General, which is 20 percent owned by PepsiCo Inc., will continue to look to acquire additional Pepsi-Cola franchises and to grow through the introduction of new beverages.

"The real opportunity for Whitman is domestically," said Prudential Securities analyst George Thompson. "That's possible with the acquisition of other Pepsi franchises, and I think they're pretty well positioned to do that."
In 1996, Pepsi-Cola General had a record operating profit of $212 million, up from $198 million a year ago.
Internationally, Pepsi-Cola General is doing business in half of Poland and in January began operations around St. Petersburg, Russia. In March, it entered the Baltics.
Analysts estimated the value of Whitman's bottling operation at $18 to $19 a share, Hussmann at $6 to $8 a share, and Midas at $4 to $5 a share.

Both Midas and Hussmann are large enough to be publicly traded companies with a single focus, analysts said, although Hussmann appeared to have the stronger fundamentals. In 1996, Hussmann's operating profit was $94 million, up from $79 million a year ago.

Midas, however, continues to face tough competition and soft consumer demand for automotive repair services. This is due, in part, to a lower rate of replacement for stainless steel mufflers. To combat those trends, Midas is trying to market additional auto maintenance services, Connolly said.
Midas, with more than 2,500 locations in 17 countries, had an operating profit in 1996 of $78 million in 1996, down from $82.5 million a year ago.
Whitman said it expects to take charges against income later this year related to the spin-offs. The size or timing of the charges was not known.
Whitman said its board also authorised the repurchase of an additional 5 million shares of its common stock.

Whitman said it expects second-quarter earnings to be about 6 cents a share below the year-ago period, due to weakness at Midas and Pepsi-Cola General Bottlers. In the 1996 quarter Whitman earned about $42 million, or 39 cents a share, on sales of $772 million.
Whitman earned $139 million, or $1.31 a share, on revenues of $3.1 billion last year.
